edited_rows.rationale: The li-Shlomo title sits inside MT verse 1 (web:Ps.72.0 = oshb:Ps.72.1) and opens straight into a petition: the imperative תֵּ֑ן (oshb:Ps.72.1), “give,” asks God to give the king God’s own justice — “God, give the king your justice; your righteousness to the royal son.” (web:Ps.72.1) The verb chain then runs third-person masculine singular about the king — יִשְׁפֹּ֤ט, ‘he will judge’ (oshb:Ps.72.4) — through the close of verse 4. Verse 5 turns the subject plural and addresses God directly (they shall fear you, oshb:Ps.72.5), which is where this strophe ends.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe to cover the whole royal-dominion movement, through the close of the nations'-homage material, was rejected because the 3ms-to-3mp subject shift at verse 5 is a concrete grammatical seam inside that stretch.

edited_rows.device_notes: Its rows share Psalm 72's parent unit. Its title carries the li-Shlomo label (2 psalms book-wide: 72, 127) and the psalm closes Book II (42-72).

edited_rows.rationale: Verse 5 opens on the plural יִֽירָא֥וּךָ, ‘they shall fear you’ (oshb:Ps.72.5): “They shall fear you while the sun endures; and as long as the moon, throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.72.5) The unit continues into the dominion imagery of מִיָּ֣ם עַד יָ֑ם, ‘from sea to sea’ (oshb:Ps.72.8), and closes on the nations' homage: “Yes, all kings shall fall down before him. All nations shall serve him.” (web:Ps.72.11) Verse 12 opens a new clause on the causal כִּֽי (oshb:Ps.72.12), which marks the boundary here.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding verses 5-7 (the reign’s perpetuity) and 8-11 (its territorial reach) into two separate rows was rejected: the opening verb of oshb:Ps.72.5 addresses God with a 2ms suffix (“They shall fear you”, web:Ps.72.5), not a third-person description of the king, which resumes only at verse 6; the two stretches instead share a moon-lexeme envelope — יָ֝רֵ֗חַ at oshb:Ps.72.5 and יָרֵֽחַ at oshb:Ps.72.7 (skeleton match, 10 verses book-wide) — bracketing them as one unit, and the causal כִּֽי that opens verse 12 is the nearer grammatical break.

edited_rows.device_notes: The dominion imagery here (“All nations shall serve him.” web:Ps.72.11) is answered later by “All nations will call him blessed.” (web:Ps.72.17), an inclusio bracketing the psalm's central movement.

edited_rows.rationale: The causal כִּֽי, “for” (oshb:Ps.72.12), opens a motive clause: יַ֭צִּיל, “he will deliver” (oshb:Ps.72.12), grounding the king's rule in his care for “the needy ... the poor, who has no helper.” (web:Ps.72.12) The unit runs through verse 14's ransom “from oppression and violence.” (web:Ps.72.14) closing before verse 15's jussile וִיחִ֗י, ‘and he shall live’ (oshb:Ps.72.15), which opens a new blessing formula.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Merging this three-verse motive clause with the blessing formula of 15-17 was rejected because the causal particle opening verse 12 and the jussive verb-form opening verse 15 mark two distinct clause types.

edited_rows.device_notes: This care-for-the-needy motive sits inside Book II's Elohistic stretch (42-72: YHWH 32 / Elohim 165 token occurrences, Book II only); Psalm 72 itself carries YHWH 1 / Elohim 2, texture only, no boundary weight on its own.

edited_rows.rationale: וִיחִ֗י, ‘and he shall live’ (oshb:Ps.72.15), opens a jussive blessing chain — “Men will pray for him continually. They will bless him all day long.” (web:Ps.72.15) — running through “His name endures forever ... All nations will call him blessed.” (web:Ps.72.17) The closing clause echoes verse 11's “All nations shall serve him.” (web:Ps.72.11), an inclusio that frames this strophe's own material against the sea-to-sea unit before it. Verse 18 opens the doxology proper, a distinct closing formula, so the strophe ends at 17.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Carrying the strophe through verse 18 was rejected because the doxology (“Praise be to Yahweh God,” web:Ps.72.18) is a formally distinct closing unit, not a continuation of the blessing-chain syntax of 15-17.

edited_rows.device_notes: The li-Shlomo blessing-chain closes here; the doxology and colophon that follow belong to a separate closing unit at the seam 72:20|73:1.

edited_rows.rationale: בָּר֤וּךְ, “Blessed” (oshb:Ps.72.18), opens the doxology and is repeated at the head of the next verse, וּבָר֤וּךְ (oshb:Ps.72.19): “Blessed be his glorious name forever! Let the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and amen.” (web:Ps.72.19), closing on the doubled אָ֘מֵ֥ן וְאָמֵֽן (oshb:Ps.72.19), the closing ‘amen and amen.’ Verse 20 then adds the colophon כָּלּ֥וּ תְפִלּ֑וֹת (oshb:Ps.72.20), “This ends the prayers by David, the son of Jesse.” (web:Ps.72.20), naming the Davidic collection just closed. The device inventory records baruch at both 72:18 and 72:19 and amen twice at 72:19 (2 baruch, 2 amen); book-wide the doxology inventory carries 5 entries across 4 book-boundaries, and only 1 of 4 (Book II, 72:18-19) shows the doubled 2-baruch/2-amen pattern.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the doxology (18-19) from the colophon (20) into separate rows was rejected because, although the device inventory keeps the doxology and colophon as distinct classes, it supports one shared coda span (72:18-20) covering both, closing Book II and the Davidic prayer-collection together.

edited_rows.rationale: The mizmor le-Asaph title sits inside MT verse 1 (web:Ps.73.0 = oshb:Ps.73.1) and states the psalm's thesis on אַ֤ךְ ט֭וֹב, ‘surely good’ (oshb:Ps.73.1): “Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.” (web:Ps.73.1) Verse 2 pivots to the speaker with the fronted pronoun וַאֲנִ֗י, ‘but as for me’ (oshb:Ps.73.2, carries a ketiv/qere pair at נטוי/נָטָ֣יוּ and שפכה/שֻׁפְּכ֥וּ, not quoted here), and verse 3 supplies the cause with “For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” (web:Ps.73.3) Verse 4 opens a new causal clause describing that envy's object, where this strophe ends.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading verse 1 alone as the title-plus-thesis row was rejected because the fronted independent pronoun opening verse 2 is the psalm's own pivot into the personal crisis that verse 3 explains, not a separate unit.

edited_rows.device_notes: All rows of Psalm 73 belong to a single parent unit. The psalm opens the Asaph collection (73-83, 12 psalms book-wide) and Book III (73-89); its own YHWH/Elohim count (1/3) sits inside Book III's 44/46 texture.

edited_rows.rationale: Verse 4 opens כִּ֤י אֵ֖ין, ‘for there are no’ (oshb:Ps.73.4), describing the wicked's ease: “For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm.” (web:Ps.73.4) The description runs through their arrogance to שַׁתּ֣וּ בַשָּׁמַ֣יִם, ‘they have set ... in the heavens’ (oshb:Ps.73.9): “They have set their mouth in the heavens. Their tongue walks through the earth.” (web:Ps.73.9) Verse 10 opens on לָכֵ֤ן, “therefore” (oshb:Ps.73.10), the same consequence particle that already opens verse 6 within this description (oshb:Ps.73.6); the boundary rests not on the particle alone but on the topical shift from the wicked's own description to others' reaction toward them, which closes this strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe through verse 12's summary (“Behold, these are the wicked”, web:Ps.73.12) was rejected because verse 10's own consequence particle opens its own clause distinct from the preceding description.

edited_rows.device_notes: The particle אך occurs in 3 verses of this psalm (73:1, 73:13, 73:18; sweep: skeleton אך, 3 verses) but is verse-initial in only 2 (73:13, 73:18) — at 73:1 it follows the mizmor-le-Asaph superscription; neither verse-initial occurrence falls in this strophe.

edited_rows.rationale: לָכֵ֤ן, “therefore” (oshb:Ps.73.10, carries a ketiv/qere pair at ישיב/יָשׁ֣וּב, not quoted here), draws the consequence — “their people return to them, and they drink up waters of abundance” (web:Ps.73.10) — and the unit closes on the summary “Behold, these are the wicked. Being always at ease, they increase in riches.” (web:Ps.73.12) The same consequence particle also opens oshb:Ps.73.6; the seam here rests on the topical shift from the wicked's own description to this reaction toward them, not the particle alone. Verse 13 restarts on the second אך (oshb:Ps.73.13), a distinct asseverative opening the speaker's own crisis, which is where this strophe ends.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating verse 12's “behold” summary as the opening of the next unit rather than the close of this one was rejected because it recapitulates “the wicked” (web:Ps.73.12) named through 4-11, not the personal crisis that follows.

edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the crisis (13-16) from the sanctuary turn (17) into separate rows was rejected because verse 17's own ‘until’-clause binds them into one sentence in the source text.

You throw them down to destruction.” (web:Ps.73.18) The unit runs through the dream-simile of verse 20 — “As a dream when one wakes up ... you will despise their fantasies.” (web:Ps.73.20) — before verse 21's כִּ֭י, “for” (oshb:Ps.73.21), turns to the speaker's own inward state, which closes this strophe.

edited_rows.rationale: כִּ֭י, “for” (oshb:Ps.73.21), opens the speaker's confession, itself reopening with the fronted pronoun וַאֲנִי (oshb:Ps.73.22) — “I was so senseless and ignorant. I was a brute beast before you.” (web:Ps.73.22) — before the fronted pronoun returns at וַאֲנִ֣י, ‘but I’ (oshb:Ps.73.23), the same construction that opened the crisis at verse 2, now reversed: “Nevertheless, I am continually with you. You have held my right hand.” (web:Ps.73.23) The psalm closes on a fourth such pivot, וַאֲנִ֤י (oshb:Ps.73.28): “But it is good for me to come close to God.” (web:Ps.73.28) Ps 73 has 28 verses in both witnesses; no further verse follows, and the strophe runs to the psalm's end.

edited_rows.device_notes: This block recounts the sanctuary's desecration in the third person, between the community's imperative petition (1-3) and its own first-person crisis statement (9-11); its own 'signs' language (plene אוֹתֹתָ֣ם and defective אֹתֽוֹת at oshb:Ps.74.4) recurs across the seam, opening oshb:Ps.74.9 (אֽוֹתֹתֵ֗ינוּ, 'our signs').

edited_rows.rationale: אֽוֹתֹתֵ֗ינוּ, ‘our signs’ (oshb:Ps.74.9), opens a first-person-plural admission that answers, negated, the same root already used twice at oshb:Ps.74.4 for the enemies' own standards (plene אוֹתֹתָ֣ם, defective אֹתֽוֹת): “We see no miraculous signs. There is no longer any prophet” (web:Ps.74.9). The unit continues on twin interrogatives, עַד מָתַ֣י, “how long” (oshb:Ps.74.10), and לָ֤מָּה, “why” (oshb:Ps.74.11, carries a ketiv/qere pair at חוקך/חֵֽיקְךָ֣, not quoted here) — the same interrogative that opened the psalm at verse 1. Verse 12 turns to a hymnic recital of God's own past acts, closing this strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Carrying this crisis-question unit through verse 17 was rejected because verse 12 opens on an adversative pivot into praise (‘yet God’), distinct in mood from the interrogatives of 9-11.

Plead your own cause.” (web:Ps.74.22) The psalm closes on “The tumult of those who rise up against you ascends continually.” (web:Ps.74.23) Ps 74 has 23 verses in both witnesses; no further verse follows.

edited_rows.rationale: Verse 2 continues a first-person divine oracle: after the verse's own opening causal particle, it carries אֲ֝נִ֗י, “I” (web:Ps.75.2 = oshb:Ps.75.3, the pronoun stands mid-verse, word 4 of 6): “When I choose the appointed time, I will judge blamelessly.” (web:Ps.75.2) The same voice continues with אָנֹכִ֨י, “I” (web:Ps.75.3 = oshb:Ps.75.4): “The earth and all its inhabitants quake. I firmly hold its pillars. Selah.” (web:Ps.75.3) and is framed explicitly by the quotative אָמַ֣רְתִּי, ‘I said’ (web:Ps.75.4 = oshb:Ps.75.5), which introduces direct speech to the arrogant: “Don't boast!” (web:Ps.75.4) The quoted speech closes at verse 5's “Don't speak with a stiff neck.” (web:Ps.75.5) Verse 6 shifts to third-person reflection about God, closing this strophe at the oracle's own frame.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading verses 2-3 as the psalmist's own vow rather than a divine oracle was rejected: their own first-person singular content (setting the appointed time, holding the pillars firm) already marks them as oracle speech distinct from the congregation's plural thanksgiving in verse 1, and the quotative frame at verse 4 (“I said to the arrogant”, web:Ps.75.4) governs the speech that follows it, addressed to the arrogant and wicked, rather than retroactively marking what precedes it.

edited_rows.rationale: The row opens just after the Selah closing the recital of wonders (web:Ps.77.15 = oshb:Ps.77.16, “סֶֽלָה”), shifting register from confessional address to vivid theophany description: “The waters saw you, God. The waters saw you, and they writhed” (web:Ps.77.16), matching “רָ֘א֤וּךָ מַּ֨יִם אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים רָא֣וּךָ מַּ֣יִם יָחִ֑ילוּ” (oshb:Ps.77.17), with the clause repeated within the verse. Storm imagery continues through web:Ps.77.17-18 (“The clouds poured out water… The voice of your thunder was in the whirlwind…”) and the sea-crossing motif at web:Ps.77.19 (“Your way was through the sea… Your footsteps were not known”), matching the ketiv/qere pair “ושביליך/וּֽ֭שְׁבִֽילְךָ” (oshb:Ps.77.20), the qere reading 'your paths', before the psalm ends at web:Ps.77.20, “You led your people like a flock, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” The Hebrew reads “בְּֽיַד מֹשֶׁ֥ה וְאַהֲרֹֽן” (oshb:Ps.77.21) -- itself still second-person address (נָחִ֣יתָ, 'you led', and עַמֶּ֑ךָ, 'your people', both 2ms). No doxology or refrain follows the Moses/Aaron notice; the psalm ends on this unresolved theophany image rather than a return to pure third-person narrative.
